name: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia
aliases: nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: Characterised by diffuse transformation of the liver into small regenerative nodules without the bridging fibrosis of cirrhosis
It is an important cause of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, often presenting with varices or splenomegaly while synthetic function and enzymes remain near normal
The typical biochemical picture is portal hypertension with preserved liver function, which should prompt consideration of the diagnosis

It is associated with autoimmune and connective tissue disorders, myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disease, HIV, and certain drugs including thiopurines and some chemotherapeutic and antiretroviral agents
Imaging can be normal or show only subtle nodularity, so the diagnosis is frequently missed and often requires liver biopsy
Histology shows regenerative nodules without fibrous septa, best appreciated on reticulin staining, distinguishing it from cirrhosis
Management focuses on treating portal hypertension and its complications and removing any causative drug or treating the underlying condition
Overall hepatic prognosis is generally better than in cirrhosis because liver function tends to be maintained
reference.pathophysiology: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia is thought to arise from heterogeneous perfusion of the hepatic parenchyma due to obliteration or narrowing of small portal veins and sinusoids. Areas losing portal inflow atrophy, while adjacent regions with preserved blood supply undergo compensatory hyperplasia, generating diffuse small regenerative nodules unaccompanied by significant fibrosis. The resulting distortion increases intrahepatic vascular resistance at a presinusoidal or sinusoidal level, producing portal hypertension despite an otherwise structurally near-normal liver. The vascular injury is linked to prothrombotic and immune-mediated states, myeloproliferative disorders, and endothelial toxicity from certain drugs, which explains its many disease associations.
additionalDifferentials: Focal nodular hyperplasia and other nodular lesions
additionalInvestigations: Liver biopsy with reticulin staining to demonstrate nodules without fibrosis
Cross-sectional imaging and Doppler assessment of the portal system
Upper endoscopy to screen for varices
Screening for associated autoimmune, haematological, and prothrombotic disorders
Review of drug exposures, including thiopurines and relevant chemotherapeutic and antiretroviral agents
Hepatic venous pressure measurement in selected cases
redFlags: Acute variceal haemorrhage requiring urgent management
Signs of an underlying myeloproliferative or lymphoproliferative disorder
Development of ascites or other decompensation
reference.prognosis: The hepatic outlook is usually favourable because synthetic function is preserved and the condition does not typically progress to cirrhosis; prognosis is chiefly determined by the complications of portal hypertension and by any associated systemic or haematological disease.
pitfalls: Labelling the disorder as cirrhosis and giving an inappropriately poor prognosis
Relying on imaging alone, which may appear normal, and missing the diagnosis
Failing to identify and withdraw a causative drug
Not investigating for an underlying autoimmune, haematological, or prothrombotic condition
